The baroness’s fishing event is the central scene of chapter fourteen and a key episode in Dietrich’s storyline. For the lieutenant, it means secretly spending money on a miracle that should solve his problems; for the reader, it is the first detailed depiction of how Dangarians use their schönbruns.

Preparations (ch. 10–14)

Elsa von Walbrecht, a wealthy, beautiful, and unattached baroness, holds an annual fishing event in her Beautiful Well on the last day of the holy month. The theme is ailments of the heart; a ticket costs two hundred marks. The mansion is styled as a steamship, with columns resembling funnels, cabin-like windows, and a paddle wheel in the pond. The well stands in a round white pavilion with stained-glass windows, containing a small theater with velvet seats and a mirrored ceiling: each spectator looks into the well through an individual mirror.

Dietrich learns of the event from a newspaper article. He secretly takes two hundred marks from the family’s hiding place behind a mirror and hires the cheapest carriage, drawn by stones. Mari is thrifty, putting exactly one week’s allowance in her purse once a week without checking the hiding place, so she has not yet noticed the missing money.

The session (ch. 14)

The fishing is led by first-rank master fisherman Fritjof Joriksen, wearing a white cloak and a white tricorne edged in gold; beneath the cloak, he wears a foreign naval uniform with many pockets. Wiglaf, who has an anchor tattoo, assists him. The master asks everyone to write on a slip of paper what “heartache” they wish to be rid of, warning that they could accidentally remove a love they need. Dietrich does not know what to ask for and writes down a foolish wish.

The session then follows a maritime ritual. The master checks the date, time, weather, and number of people “aboard” according to the sea reckoning, and announces that there are thirty-six when there should be thirty-five: one is “extra,” and his gaze singles out Dietrich. Dietrich is ready to leave, but the baroness insists that in that case she will go herself, so he stays, ashamed. Joriksen produces powder, a potion, a bone, flint, and steel, burns the slips, and removes the lid.

Through the mirrors, the spectators see that instead of a schönbrun’s usual mist, the water is so clear that the bottom is visible: a red-and-gold meadow with crabs the size of horses. Out of malice, the crabs destroy the meadow, tearing cracks in the earth that become ravines and swallow the monsters themselves; the meadow then knits together and sways in the wind again. The master announces that the fishing has succeeded.

The ball and conversations (ch. 14)

Euphoria takes hold of the guests, each expressing it differently. At the table, the baroness introduces three guests: Joriksen; Count Friedrich von Wahrheit, owner of four newspapers, including Glory; and Prince Wladyslaw Lenz, marshal of the Latsen Voivodeship’s nobility, who has come with his niece Olkha. Dietrich recognizes her as the young woman he met in occupied Latsen. An Ollandian prince’s presence in Hofstadt provokes a dragoon cornet’s insult, but Dietrich defuses the quarrel with a toast to recent enemies who will become allies. Count Wahrheit supports him, while the cornet nurses a grudge.

Dietrich catches up with Joriksen by the pond and tries to buy his services, calling the well in Ollandia “his own.” The master refuses: paupers do not own schönbruns, he is no tradesman, and he works only with well owners. Later, in the smoking room, a millionaire merchant assures Prince Lenz that the war will soon end, that its main purpose is to open a route into Catalia, and proposes buying land for the railway. During a waltz, the cornet takes Olkha away from her partner.

In the evening, players at the card game shtoss discuss the “terrible incident” in Dunkwald: fishermen and officers have died. Count Wahrheit replies that Glory does not print nonsense. Then the bell rings for the “feeding”: nobles stand behind their stone servants, the formula “we care for you” is spoken, and each puts the last spoonful directly into a servant’s mouth. Dietrich is moved, while Olkha whispers her outrage at the hypocrisy and slavery. Dietrich explains that the Sower commanded people to care for one another, that everyone fed everyone else in the Silver Kingdom, and that the ritual remains as a “victory of the stones,” won by force of arms in the Wars of the Three Kingdoms. Olkha slips him an address card and asks him to visit on Saturday.

In the gazebo, Dietrich overhears Joriksen and the baroness discussing the deaths of guild members and the magnus’s fury. He then announces that he has discovered a schönbrun in Ollandia unknown to the guild. Joriksen does not believe him: none has been found in half a century. But when Dietrich describes his “spontaneous fishing”—a faceless man with a mouth in his belly and a pack of small beasts—the master believes him and invites him to his home.

Consequences (ch. 14–29)

At home, Mari, having found the hiding place empty, is relieved that the money is safe, then horrified at how little remains. Dietrich confesses that he asked “for Mari to love me as much as I love her.” Horrified, Mari calls it an attack on their family, then breaks into tears: she already loves him, and that did not require a fishing session.

The fishing event connects Dietrich to the principal forces in the novel’s second half. Joriksen becomes his business partner in chapter twenty-one, Olkha his beloved (ch. 17–29), and Prince Lenz emerges as the owner of the land containing the well near the railway halt. In chapter twenty-nine, Count von Lurd includes the fishing event among the circumstances that could make Lenz “unreliable”: in his account, the Ollandian prince tried to use magic to marry his niece to a Dangarian grandee, but the niece directed the magic at the wrong person—a modest young man.
